title: The Shrewd Manager and the Rich Man and Lazarus
summary: Jesus tells of a manager who, about to be dismissed, reduces his master's debtors' bills to win friends, and draws lessons about using money faithfully and the impossibility of serving both God and money. When the money-loving Pharisees scoff, he answers them about self-justification, the Law, the kingdom, and divorce, then tells the story of a rich man who ignored a beggar named Lazarus at his gate and found the roles reversed after death.
story:
Luke's long account of Jesus' travel toward Jerusalem continues (9:51-19:27). Chapter 15 ended with three parables of lost things found, told to Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that Jesus ate with sinners. Now Jesus turns to his disciples, with the Pharisees still listening (verse 14), and speaks about money, a subject Luke returns to more than any other Gospel writer: Mary's song of the hungry filled and the rich sent away empty (1:53), the blessings and woes of the Sermon on the Plain (6:20-26), the rich fool (12:13-21), and, still to come, the rich ruler (18:18-30) and Zacchaeus (19:1-10).

The chapter is framed by two parables that begin with the same Greek words, ‘a certain man was rich’ (verses 1 and 19). The first shows a man who uses what passes through his hands with an eye on his future; the second shows a man who used his wealth with no eye on anything beyond his own table. The verb used of the younger son who squandered his inheritance (diaskorpizō, 15:13) returns in verse 1: the manager too is accused of scattering his master's possessions. Between the two parables stands a short, dense set of sayings (verses 14-18) that answer the Pharisees' scoffing: God knows the heart, the kingdom now being preached does not cancel the Law, and the Law's claim reaches as far as marriage. The last line, that some will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead, looks ahead to Easter and to the unbelief that follows it in Acts.
historical:
Large estates in Galilee and Judea were often owned by wealthy landlords, some living in cities or abroad, and run by managers (oikonomoi) who handled rents, loans, and contracts on their behalf. Such a manager might be a slave or a freedman with wide legal power to act in his master's name, which is why the debtors accept his changes without question. Tenants and borrowers often owed in produce, so the debts are measured in olive oil and wheat. The Greek units are the batos, the Hebrew bath, and the koros, the Hebrew cor, which held ten baths (Ezekiel 45:14). Modern estimates of the bath range from about 22 to about 40 liters (roughly 6 to 10 gallons), so a cor was somewhere between about 220 and 400 liters. A hundred baths of oil and a hundred cors of wheat are large commercial quantities. Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus, German 1947) estimated that the two reductions, fifty baths of oil and twenty cors of wheat, were worth about the same, roughly five hundred denarii each, well over a laborer's yearly wage.

What exactly the manager did is disputed, and the answer shapes the parable. J. Duncan M. Derrett (Fresh Light on St Luke xvi, New Testament Studies 7, 1961) argued that the bills included interest that the Law of Moses forbade Jews to charge one another (Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:36-37, Deuteronomy 23:19-20) and that was hidden by writing the loan in commodities; by cancelling it the manager made his master look righteous, and the master could only agree. Joseph A. Fitzmyer (The Story of the Dishonest Manager, Theological Studies 25, 1964) developed a related view: the manager struck out his own commission, the amount he had added to each bill for himself, so that he sacrificed his short-term gain to secure friends. John S. Kloppenborg (The Dishonoured Master, Biblica 70, 1989) questioned whether the reductions match known interest rates in Egyptian loan documents and read the story through the honor culture of the Mediterranean: a master already shamed by a wasteful manager is now publicly praised for generosity he never intended, and cannot reverse the reductions without losing face. Others, including Jeremias, take the story at face value: the manager cheated his master a second time, and Jesus praises his decisiveness, not his morals.

The saying on divorce (verse 18) enters a live debate. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 assumes that a man may divorce his wife if he finds ‘some indecency’ in her and gives her a written certificate. The Mishnah (m. Gittin 9:10) remembers the school of Shammai limiting this to sexual unfaithfulness, the school of Hillel allowing divorce if she spoiled his food, and Rabbi Akiva allowing it even if he found another woman more beautiful. Josephus, writing in the 90s, paraphrases the law as permitting divorce for any cause whatever (Antiquities 4.253) and mentions divorcing his own wife because he was displeased with her behavior (Life 426). Under Jewish law as the rabbis later framed it, the husband gave the certificate; Josephus calls it contrary to Jewish law when Herod's sister Salome sent one to her husband Costobarus (Antiquities 15.259-260), though Jewish marriage contracts from Elephantine in the fifth century BC allowed a wife to initiate divorce, and Roman law allowed either spouse to do so, which is why Mark 10:12 addresses a wife who divorces. The Damascus Document from Qumran (CD 4:20-5:2) already criticized taking a second wife while the first was living, appealing to Genesis 1:27. Jesus' saying, stricter than either school, treats the husband's remarriage as adultery against his wife, a startling claim in a world where adultery was defined as an offense against a husband.
cultural:
Jesus calls money mammon (verses 9, 11, and 13), from an Aramaic and late Hebrew word for wealth or property. It is absent from the Hebrew Bible but appears in the Hebrew text of Sirach 31:8, in the Damascus Document from Qumran (CD 14:20), and in the Mishnah (m. Avot 2:12, which urges that a neighbor's property be as dear to you as your own). The phrase ‘mammon of unrighteousness’ (verse 9, BSB “worldly wealth”) probably means wealth as it belongs to this unrighteous age, not money gained by fraud. ‘Sons of light’ (verse 8) was a self-description of the community at Qumran, whose Rule (1QS 1:9-10) tells members to love all the sons of light and hate the sons of darkness, and whose War Scroll imagines the final battle between them; Paul uses similar language (1 Thessalonians 5:5, Ephesians 5:8).

Luke's note that the Pharisees were ‘lovers of money’ (philarguroi, verse 14) is a charge, not a description of the whole movement. Josephus says the Pharisees lived simply and scorned luxury (Antiquities 18.12), and the rabbis who inherited their tradition warned sharply against the love of wealth. The charge echoes common ancient polemic against teachers who used religion for gain (compare 1 Timothy 6:5, 2 Timothy 3:2), and it goes with the complaint that they justify themselves before others (verse 15). The assumption Jesus overturns, that prosperity signals God's favor, was widespread in the ancient world and finds some support in Proverbs and Deuteronomy; Job and the Psalms (Psalm 73) had already complicated it.

In the second parable the rich man wears purple, cloth dyed with an expensive extract from murex sea snails and associated with royalty, and fine linen (bussos), costly cloth often imported from Egypt. He feasts ‘every day’, while most people ate meat only at festivals. Lazarus lies at his pulōn, the gateway of a large house with a courtyard, perhaps carried and left there (the verb is passive, ‘had been laid’). Dogs in that world were scavengers, not pets, and their licking his sores makes his helplessness and uncleanness vivid. Lazarus is the Greek form of Eleazar, ‘God has helped’. He is the only named character in any of Jesus' parables. Burial is noted only for the rich man (verse 22), perhaps implying a grand funeral, while the beggar's body may have gone unburied.

‘Abraham's side’ (literally his bosom, kolpos) pictures the place of honor at a banquet, where a guest reclined against the chest of the one beside him (John 13:23), and more broadly the rest of the righteous with the patriarchs; 4 Maccabees 13:17 has the martyred brothers expect Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to receive them. Hades was the Greek name for the realm of the dead, and the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made in the centuries before Jesus) used it for the Hebrew Sheol. Jewish writings of the period described the dead as held in separate places until the judgment: 1 Enoch 22 describes hollow places in the west where the spirits of the righteous are kept near a bright spring of water and the wicked apart from them. Stories of a rich man and a poor man whose fortunes are reversed after death circulated widely, in Egypt and in Jewish tradition, as the interpretation section below explains.
literary:
The chapter pairs two parables, both opening with ‘a certain man was rich’, around a short set of sayings (verses 14-18) that respond to the Pharisees' scoffing. The first parable (verses 1-8a) turns on an inner speech, a device Luke uses in several parables (12:17-19, 15:17-19, 18:4-5): ‘What shall I do?’ The manager's crisis, his calculation, and his quick action come in brisk sequence. The story ends with the master's surprising praise, and then a chain of sayings (8b-13) loosely linked by catchwords: shrewd, unrighteous, wealth, faithful, little and much, another's and your own, master and servant. C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) remarked that these verses read like notes for several sermons on the parable, and interpreters still debate where the parable ends and Jesus' or Luke's application begins, and whether ‘the master’ of verse 8 is the rich man or Jesus himself (Luke often calls Jesus ho kurios, ‘the Lord’, as in 18:6).

The sayings in verses 14-18 are compressed and connected by the theme of the Law. Verse 15 uses the verb ‘justify’ (dikaioō), which returns in 18:14, where a tax collector goes home justified and a Pharisee does not. Verses 16-17 affirm both that a new era began with John and that the Law stands, and verse 18 gives an example of the Law's force intensified rather than relaxed.

The second parable (verses 19-31) falls into two scenes, life (19-21) and death (22-31), with a reversal between them. Its first half is built on contrasts: purple and linen against sores, a daily feast against crumbs, a gate that divides them, a burial against no burial. After death the positions reverse, and the gate becomes a great chasm. The rich man speaks three times, each time still treating Lazarus as someone to be sent on errands, and Abraham answers three times. The first answer (verse 25) echoes Mary's song and the beatitudes and woes (1:52-53, 6:20-25). The second and third move the story from the fate of the dead to the living brothers, and the parable ends not with a verdict on the rich man but with a warning to the listeners: “If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.” The Pharisees, who had Moses and the prophets, are left in the position of the five brothers.

outline.t: The parable of the shrewd manager
Faithfulness with money; God or money
The Pharisees scoff; the Law, the kingdom, and divorce
The rich man and Lazarus in life
The reversal after death and the great chasm
The request for the brothers: Moses and the prophets

doctrines.note: The chapter treats money as a rival master that claims service: “You cannot serve both God and money” (verse 13). It also treats money as a trust to be used for others with eternity in view (verses 9-12). The rich man's sin is not described as fraud but as a daily feast beside an ignored beggar.

The parable of the rich man and Lazarus pictures persons conscious and recognizable after death, before the resurrection, in contrasting conditions (verses 22-26). How literally to take its imagery is debated, but it is the New Testament's most extended picture of the state of the dead, and it shows a separation that cannot be crossed.

Jesus affirms that a new era of preaching the kingdom began with John, and in the same breath that not the smallest stroke of the Law will fail (verses 16-17). His saying on divorce (verse 18) shows the Law's intent pressed deeper, not set aside.

In a world where a husband could dismiss a wife at will, Jesus treats remarriage after such a divorce as adultery (verse 18), protecting the permanence of the marriage covenant and the wife who could otherwise be discarded.

Abraham's answer, “They have Moses and the prophets; let your brothers listen to them” (verse 29), presents Scripture as sufficient to call people to repentance, and warns that a miracle will not persuade those who refuse the word already given (verse 31).

words.note: Oikonomos, manager or steward, one who runs a household (oikos) or estate for its owner. It occurs 10 times in the New Testament, four in Luke (12:42 and three times here, verses 1, 3, and 8), and the related noun oikonomia, ‘management’, three times in verses 2-4. The word later becomes a picture of Christian responsibility: Paul calls himself and Apollos stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1-2), and 1 Peter 4:10 calls believers stewards of God's varied grace. The parable's point rests here: what we hold is not ours but our master's, and we will give account for it.

Mamōnas, wealth, from an Aramaic word for money or property. It occurs only four times in the New Testament, three of them in this chapter (verses 9, 11, 13) and once in the parallel saying of Matthew 6:24. The etymology is uncertain; a derivation from the root ‘to trust’ (that in which one trusts) has been proposed but is not secure, and no doctrine should rest on it. What matters is the use: Jesus personifies wealth as a master competing for service, which is why older translations kept the word Mammon. The BSB renders it “worldly wealth” and “money”.

Phronimōs, shrewdly, prudently, occurs only here (verse 8). The adjective phronimos, ‘prudent, sensible’, occurs 14 times in the New Testament, seven in Matthew, where it describes the wise man who built on rock (Matthew 7:24), the faithful and wise servant (24:45), and the wise virgins (25:2). In Luke 12:42 it is the faithful and prudent manager. The standard lexicon (BDAG) gives the sense of practical wisdom, acting sensibly in view of a situation. The manager is praised for this quality, not for dishonesty; the narrator calls him ‘the manager of unrighteousness’ (verse 8).

Philarguros, fond of money, avaricious, occurs only twice in the New Testament: of the Pharisees here (verse 14) and in the list of vices of the last days in 2 Timothy 3:2. The related noun philarguria is ‘a root of all kinds of evil’ in 1 Timothy 6:10. It was a stock charge in ancient moral writing against philosophers and teachers who profited from their teaching. Luke uses it to explain why the Pharisees scoffed: the teaching on money struck home.

Biazō, to force, use violence, and in the middle voice to press or force one's way. It occurs twice in the New Testament, here and in the parallel Matthew 11:12, where its sense is famously disputed. In verse 16 the BSB reads “everyone is forcing his way into it”, meaning the eager rush of people like tax collectors into the kingdom. Other interpreters take the verb as passive, ‘everyone is urged insistently to enter it’, which fits Luke's emphasis on the preaching. Either way, the kingdom is being entered now, not merely awaited.

Moicheuō, to commit adultery, occurs 15 times in the New Testament, three in Luke (16:18 twice and 18:20, the commandment). In the Old Testament adultery was a man's intercourse with another man's wife, an offense against her husband. Jesus' saying applies the word to a husband who divorces and remarries, making him an offender against his own wife, which reframes the offense in terms of the marriage covenant itself.

Hadēs, the realm of the dead. It occurs 10 times in the New Testament: in Luke only here and at 10:15, twice in Acts 2 (quoting Psalm 16), twice in Matthew, and four times in Revelation, where Christ holds its keys (1:18) and it is finally thrown into the lake of fire (20:14). In the Septuagint it translates Sheol, the place of all the dead. Here it is a place of torment separated from Abraham's side. The New Testament uses a different word, Gehenna, for final punishment (12:5), and interpreters debate whether Hades here means the intermediate state or anticipates final judgment.

Kolpos, bosom, chest, lap, and by extension the fold of a garment. It occurs six times in the New Testament, including here (verses 22 and 23, where the BSB has “Abraham's side”), of the beloved disciple reclining at Jesus' side (John 13:23), and of the Son who is at the Father's side (John 1:18). The picture is of intimacy and honor at a banquet. ‘Abraham's bosom’ became a standard Christian name for the rest of the righteous dead.

christ:
The chapter's last line carries a shadow of what is coming. Abraham says that those who will not listen to Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. Luke's readers knew that someone did rise, and that many still did not believe. In chapter 24 the risen Jesus himself points his disciples back to Moses and all the Prophets to explain his death and resurrection (24:25-27, 24:44-47), and in Acts the apostles preach the resurrection from those same Scriptures. The parable does not end with a messenger from the dead; it ends by sending its hearers back to the word, which is where the risen Christ also sends them. John's Gospel tells of a real Lazarus who did return from the dead, and whose raising hardened some in their resolve to kill Jesus (John 11:45-53, 12:10-11), an unplanned but striking echo of Abraham's warning.

The chapter also shows Jesus' authority over the Law. He announces that the time of the Law and the Prophets ran until John and that the kingdom is now proclaimed as good news (verse 16), yet he does not loosen the Law; not a stroke of it will fail (verse 17). He speaks with the authority to say what the Law means for marriage (verse 18), as he does elsewhere for the Sabbath (6:5). The church confesses him as the one in whom the Law and the Prophets reach their goal (24:44).

The parables about money flow from the character of Jesus' mission as Luke has announced it: good news to the poor (4:18) and a reversal in which the lowly are lifted and the rich sent away empty (1:52-53). The beggar at the gate is the kind of person Jesus told his host to invite to the banquet (14:13, 14:21). And the call to make friends with wealth that will welcome you into eternal dwellings (verse 9) is fulfilled in the one who, though rich, became poor so that others might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and whose own teaching on treasure in heaven (12:33) the chapter illustrates from both sides.
interpretation:
The dishonest manager has been called the hardest of Jesus' parables. Allegorical readers made the manager a model: Jerome (Letter 121, to Algasia) took the lesson to be that if a steward of unrighteous wealth is praised for prudence, Christ's disciples should use wealth for the poor so as to be received into eternal dwellings, and almsgiving became the standard application through the Middle Ages. Luther and Calvin read verses 8-9 the same way, and Calvin warned against pressing every detail of a parable. In Lutheran Leipzig, Luke 16:1-9 was the Gospel for the Ninth Sunday after Trinity, and Bach's cantatas Herr, gehe nicht ins Gericht (BWV 105, 1723), Was frag ich nach der Welt (BWV 94, 1724), and Tue Rechnung, Donnerwort (BWV 168, 1725) were written for it.

Modern study has produced several readings. Jeremias read it as a crisis parable: the manager acted decisively when his future was at stake, and so must Jesus' hearers. Derrett (1961) and Fitzmyer (1964) argued that the manager removed usurious interest or his own commission, so that he became honest. D. R. Fletcher (The Riddle of the Unjust Steward: Is Irony the Key?, Journal of Biblical Literature 82, 1963) and others read verses 8-9 as irony, as if Jesus said, ‘go ahead, make friends with mammon and see whether they can receive you into eternal homes’. Kenneth Bailey (Poet and Peasant, 1976) argued that the manager gambled on his master's generosity, which the master chose to uphold. Kloppenborg (1989) read it as a story of a master shamed and forced into generosity. William Herzog (Parables as Subversive Speech, 1994) saw the manager as a retainer caught between elite and peasants.

The rich man and Lazarus has two famous ancient parallels. The first is Egyptian. A Demotic papyrus in the British Museum (EA 10822), written on the back of Greek land registers dated to the seventh year of Claudius (AD 46/47), tells how Setne Khamwas and his son Si-Osire watch the lavish funeral of a rich man and the pauper's burial of a poor man. Si-Osire leads his father through the halls of the underworld, where the poor man, whose good deeds outweighed his bad, stands near Osiris clothed in the rich man's fine linen, while the rich man lies with the pivot of the underworld's door fixed in his right eye. Hugo Gressmann (Vom reichen Mann und armen Lazarus, 1918) argued that Jewish storytellers had taken up this tale. The second is Jewish. The Jerusalem Talmud (y. Hagigah 2:2, 77d; y. Sanhedrin 6:9, 23c) tells of the tax collector Bar Ma'yan in Ashkelon, who received a splendid funeral, and a poor pious man who died unmourned; in a dream a friend sees the pious man in gardens beside springs of water, and Bar Ma'yan on a riverbank, his tongue stretched out toward the water but unable to reach it. Richard Bauckham (The Rich Man and Lazarus: The Parable and the Parallels, New Testament Studies 37, 1991) showed that Jesus uses two familiar motifs, a reversal after death and a messenger from the dead, and then refuses the second: no one will be sent. Outi Lehtipuu (The Afterlife Imagery in Luke's Story of the Rich Man and Lazarus, 2007) set the imagery in the wider Greek and Roman world.

Irenaeus (Against Heresies 2.34.1) used the parable to show that souls survive death, keep their form, and remember, and Tertullian (On the Soul 7) argued from the rich man's tongue that the soul is in some sense bodily; in Against Marcion 4.34 he distinguished Abraham's bosom from the place of torment. John Chrysostom preached a series of sermons on it at Antioch (in English as On Wealth and Poverty, 1984), pressing that failing to share with the poor is a kind of theft. Medieval theology identified Abraham's bosom with the limbo of the fathers. The Latin dives, ‘rich man’, became the name Dives. The parable is carved on the south porch of Moissac (about 1115-1130) and painted in the Codex Aureus of Echternach (about 1035-1040). It is the English carol Dives and Lazarus (Child ballad 56), which Vaughan Williams set as Five Variants of Dives and Lazarus (1939). Luke 16:19-31 was the Gospel for the First Sunday after Trinity, and Bach's first cantata as Leipzig cantor, Die Elenden sollen essen (BWV 75, 1723), was written for it. The Orthodox read it on the Fifth Sunday of Luke; the Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary read verses 1-13 and 19-31 on consecutive Sundays in September of Year C.
text:
Several differences between manuscripts affect English Bibles. In verse 19 the rich man has no name in almost all manuscripts, but P75, among the oldest copies of Luke, adds ‘by name Neues’, and the Sahidic Coptic version names him in a similar form; a Latin work attributed to Cyprian and the writer Priscillian call him Phineas. Scholars think these names arose from scribes filling a gap, and English Bibles do not print them. The name Dives is not in any manuscript; it comes from the Latin Vulgate's dives, ‘rich man’.

In verse 21 the earliest manuscripts read that Lazarus longed to be fed ‘with what fell’ from the rich man's table. Many later manuscripts add ‘the crumbs’, as in the Canaanite woman's reply in Matthew 15:27, and the King James Version follows them. The BSB also says “crumbs”, which may reflect the later text or simply render the sense. In verse 12 most manuscripts ask who will give you ‘what is your own’, but Codex Vaticanus and a few others read ‘what is ours’, and Westcott and Hort printed it; most editors judge ‘your own’ original. None of these changes the teaching of the chapter.

teach.big: Money is a trust to be used for God's purposes and for others, not a master to be served, because this life's choices carry weight beyond death and God has already spoken plainly enough in Scripture.

outline.t: When the crisis comes, the shrewd act decisively; the children of light should be at least as clear-eyed about their future as the children of this age.
Use wealth for people, be faithful in small and borrowed things, and refuse to let money become your master.
Self-justification before others cannot hide the heart from God, who reverses human ranking.
The kingdom's arrival does not loosen God's Law but presses its intent deeper, as the saying on divorce shows.
The sin of the rich man is blindness to the poor person at his own gate.
Death reveals and fixes the reality of a life; the comfort and the torment are both real.
God's word already given is enough; people who refuse it will not be moved by a miracle.

teach.pitfalls:
The shrewd manager is often preached as if Jesus approved of dishonesty or as if the parable taught clever financial strategy. The narrator calls the manager unrighteous (verse 8); the praise is for decisive foresight, and the lesson is drawn from the lesser to the greater. Equally, avoid presenting any one reconstruction (commission, interest, honor) as settled fact; each is a scholar's proposal.

The rich man and Lazarus is misused in two opposite ways. Some use it as a detailed map of the afterlife, with conversations between heaven and hell and exact geography; the story's imagery is drawn from familiar Jewish pictures and should not be pressed beyond what it plainly teaches. Others dismiss it as mere folklore with nothing to say about life after death; that ignores the story's plain point that death fixes consequences. Do not teach that Lazarus is saved because he is poor or that the rich man is condemned for being rich; the story implies the rich man's failure to heed Moses and the prophets (verses 29-31), which command care for the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7-11, Isaiah 58:7). Avoid turning the Pharisees into a caricature of Judaism; the warning falls on anyone, the church included, who has Scripture and ignores the beggar.

Verse 18 is often preached in isolation, as if it were Jesus' complete teaching on divorce. The New Testament says more (Matthew 5:32, 19:9; Mark 10:2-12; 1 Corinthians 7:10-16), and Christian traditions have read the texts together differently. Teaching the verse without that context, or without care for the divorced people present, fails both the text and the listeners.
teach.pastoral: Verse 18 will press on divorced and remarried people, on those in painful marriages, and on those who have been abandoned. Christian traditions differ: the Roman Catholic Church holds a valid sacramental marriage to be indissoluble and examines whether a marriage was valid (annulment); the Orthodox churches, by economy, permit a second marriage with a penitential rite; many Protestant confessions, following the Westminster Confession (24.5-6), allow divorce and remarriage for adultery and desertion; some evangelical scholars, such as David Instone-Brewer (Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible, 2002), argue that neglect and abuse are also grounds, while Gordon Wenham has argued that the early church allowed separation but not remarriage. Present these fairly, and do not let the verse become a weapon. The saying protected a wife from being discarded; it must never be used to keep anyone in danger. No reading of Scripture requires a person to remain where they or their children are being abused: safety comes first, and those at risk should contact local emergency services or a domestic violence hotline. This is pastoral guidance, not legal advice; people facing divorce or separation need a qualified lawyer. The parable of Lazarus may also press on those grieving loved ones who died without professed faith; the story warns the living and does not invite speculation about particular people, whom the church entrusts to the just and merciful God.

hard.q: Why would Jesus praise a dishonest manager?
hard.a:
The objection is as old as the parable. The story seems to commend fraud: a man about to be fired cheats his employer a second time and is praised for it. Modern critics have sharpened the point. Jeremias and many historical critics think the sayings in verses 8b-13 were attached to the parable because early Christians themselves were embarrassed by it and supplied several different morals, and C. H. Dodd (1935) observed that the verses read like notes for separate sermons. Readers outside the church have cited the story as evidence that the Gospels' ethics are unstable, and even sympathetic scholars such as Fletcher (1963) concluded that the plain reading is so troubling that Jesus must have meant it ironically.

Responses take several forms. The most common holds that the master, not Jesus, commends the manager, and commends his shrewdness, not his dishonesty; the narrator calls him ‘the manager of unrighteousness’. Jesus uses a scoundrel to make a point from the lesser to the greater, as he does with the unjust judge in 18:1-8: if people of this age act so decisively for a short-term future, how much more should the children of light act for an eternal one. This is the reading of Jerome, Calvin, Jeremias, and most commentators. A second response, from Derrett (1961) and Fitzmyer (1964), argues that the manager was not dishonest in the reductions at all, since he removed illegal interest or his own commission; critics such as Kloppenborg reply that the text still calls him unrighteous and that the numbers do not fit known rates. A third, from Bailey (1976), holds that the manager threw himself on his master's known generosity and that the master's praise reveals a merciful master, a picture of God. A fourth, the ironic reading, takes verse 9 as sarcasm. Each response has able defenders, and the parable has not yielded a single agreed reading; what all agree on is the chapter's own conclusion, that no one can serve both God and money.

hard.q: Is the rich man and Lazarus a literal picture of the afterlife?
hard.a:
Several objections press here. Skeptical historians such as Bart Ehrman (Heaven and Hell, 2020) argue that the story teaches immediate reward and punishment at death, that this idea appears in the Gospels only in Luke, that it differs from the resurrection hope of Jesus' own apocalyptic preaching, and that later Christian ideas of heaven and hell grew from reading a parable literally. Seventh-day Adventists, who hold that the dead sleep until the resurrection, and conditionalists such as Edward Fudge (The Fire That Consumes, 1982), who hold that the lost are finally destroyed rather than tormented forever, argue that Jesus borrowed a popular story, known from Egyptian and Jewish parallels, to make a point about wealth and Scripture without endorsing its picture of the dead. Others note the physical details (a tongue, a finger, water, fire) and the conversation across the chasm, which fit poorly with the bodiless state of souls before the resurrection.

On the other side, many Christian readers, from Irenaeus and Tertullian onward, have taken the story as teaching that the dead are conscious between death and resurrection, and they point to Jesus' promise to the criminal, ‘today you will be with me in paradise’ (23:43), and to Paul's desire to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). Some, especially in older popular teaching, read the story as history, noting that Lazarus is named. Most interpreters, including many who affirm a conscious intermediate state, read it as a parable that uses familiar Jewish imagery (Abraham's bosom, compartments of Hades) and should not be mined for a map of the unseen world; Bauckham (1991) showed how Jesus took up the common motifs and changed their point. John Calvin wrote against soul sleep (Psychopannychia, 1542), and Oscar Cullmann (Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead?, his Ingersoll Lecture of 1955, published in English in 1958) warned against Greek ideas of the soul displacing the resurrection. The church's confession of the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come is not in question; how the dead exist before that day is a question on which faithful Christians differ. What every reading shares is the story's plain teaching: God sees the poor, this life's choices matter beyond it, and there comes a point when it is too late.
